features.guide: docs/guides/getting-started.md § Step 3b — Claim a new nest
features.title: Claim a fresh nest
features.what:
A brand-new nest belongs to the first person who claims it with the one-time
code it printed when it started. Paste the code in the app and you are its owner
and admin: the app asks whether the nest lives on the open internet or behind
your home router, offers you one optional tap to trust the nest to read your
mail and calendar for itself (to check your mail again when its virus and spam checks are updated), a trust you can take back at any time, and if your handle carries a real domain, and the
nest is on the open internet, turns mail on for you without another question —
unless your nest was set up without mail.

features.title: Connect to your nest and sign in
features.what:
With your identity on the device, opening the app signs you in and shows your
feed; there is nothing to type. The app remembers which nest is yours and checks it
is really that nest every time. A nest you have just set up opens connected straight
away, without waiting for its web address to spread across the internet. If the nest
cannot be reached you get a retry, not a dead end, and if the nest is replaced
underneath you (an upgrade, a restart) the app reconnects and catches up on its own.

features.title: Create your identity
features.what:
The first thing the app does is make you a key. There is no account form, no
email address to confirm and no account password: the key is your identity, it
is created on your device, and it leaves your device only when you move it
yourself, though your device's own backup may carry it, still locked. You
confirm you have saved it and move on to choosing a handle.

features.guide: docs/guides/install.md § The no-install option: the web app
features.title: Get the app
features.what:
Every nest serves the web app itself by default, so on any device with a browser
you open your nest's address and you are in — nothing to install. The six native
apps (Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and the terminal app) are built from
source today, outside Google Play's invitation-only testing of the Android app
and the pre-release downloads of the Windows, Linux and terminal apps; public releases arrive once a version passes acceptance, and from then on the nest and every app's release channel that exists ship together at one version. The Windows installer can also set up your nest on the computer it installs on — its "Nest Service" choice, off by default — as a service that starts with the computer, runs with nobody signed in, and that your other devices reach over the network; the macOS package, once published, does the same.

features.guide: docs/guides/getting-started.md § Step 3a — Join with an invite
features.title: Join an existing nest
features.what:
Type the handle you want and the app finds the nest behind it and tells you
where you stand: already a member, welcome back; not yet, then you ask to join. An
invite code from the admin lets you straight in; without one, your request waits for
approval and the app takes you in by itself the moment it is granted. A refused
request shows you the reason and lets you ask again.

features.title: Recover a lost nest
features.what:
If the machine your nest ran on is gone for good, your app can bring it back
with the same identity, so every device and every contact that knew the old nest
carries on without a trust warning. The app keeps what it needs for that from the
moment you claim; recovery is a choice of where the new nest should run.

features.title: Recovery kit at sign-up
features.what:
Right after your identity is created, the app offers to make a recovery kit: a
second key, kept only by you and only offline, that can get your account back if
you lose your secret key, or take it back if someone steals it. You can skip it
in one tap and make one later from Settings; skipping never blocks sign-up.

features.title: Set up a nest in the cloud from the app
features.what:
You do not need to know how to run a server. Pick a domain provider and a
hosting provider, paste the keys they give you, choose a server, and watch the app
buy the domain, rent the machine, install the nest and point your domain at it. You
see every step, the price before you commit, and you can cancel or retry. If you
would rather set DNS up yourself, the app shows you exactly which records to add and
waits for them.

features.title: terms-and-content-guidelines
features.what: This text is being written and will appear here once it has been reviewed.

features.title: Use your identity on another device
features.what:
Your identity is a key, and a second device needs a copy. Settings shows it as a
code you reveal on purpose, with a warning that whoever scans it becomes you; the new
device pastes or scans it and is signed in as you. The code hides again as soon as
you are done.

features.title: Your app's version, and news of a newer one
features.what:
Settings shows which version of Fauna you are running — one version number, the
same on every app, so "what version are you on?" always has one answer. On a
computer, where you install the app yourself, you can also ask it whether a
newer version is out, and when one is, it says so and where to get it. The web
app your nest serves is always your nest's own version, and a phone app
installed from an app store is kept current by that store, so there is nothing
to ask there.

features.guide: docs/guides/calendar-and-contacts.md § Contacts: two different address books, on purpose
features.title: Address book
features.what:
A second segment of Contacts is your address book: the cards a standard contacts
app keeps on your nest. Open a card and its name, phone and email are there; the
card is stored encrypted on your nest, which opens it with the password of a
mail, calendar, contacts or file app you connect, and only for that app's
signed-in session, and the Fauna app opens it on your own device. Beyond that,
no permission you give your nest lets it read your address book. Your nest also
sees what any server that delivers your messages must: who you're connected to —
your contacts, whom you follow, the groups you're in — and when and how much you
send.

features.title: Browse, upload and manage your files
features.what:
Media shows every file in every folder you can read, or one folder at a time.
Upload into a folder, open a file's version history and restore an older one, delete
with a single confirmation, and watch a file that just synced appear without
reloading. Each item says whether it is synced.

features.title: Build your own feeds
features.what:
Make a feed from rules: posts containing a phrase, carrying a hashtag, under a
content label, and more. Weigh what ranks it, for this feed alone or for all your
feeds. Feeds you no longer want delete in one step.

features.title: Calendars and events
features.what:
Keep calendars on your nest and see them by month, week, day or as a list.
Create events from a slot, invite people by email, set a reminder, RSVP from the card
or the detail, and hide a calendar without deleting it. Your week starts on the day
your locale says, and an event added from another app appears while you are looking.

features.title: Contacts
features.what:
Your contacts page lists the people you have connected with and the knocks
waiting for you. Look someone up by their handle, send a knock, and see one arrive
while you watch. Blocking someone is a toggle on their profile.

features.title: Delete your own post
features.what:
Your own posts have a delete action behind their menu, with a confirmation. It
is gone from the feed once you confirm; other people's posts offer no such action.

features.guide: docs/guides/own-your-mail.md § Mail in the Fauna app
features.title: Email, in the same conversations
features.what:
Once mail is on, email lives in Conversations next to everything else. Write to
any address and it goes out from your own domain; replies and new mail arrive
decrypted in the same list, HTML mail renders cleanly, and pictures loaded from the
internet stay blocked until you choose. What you sent from another mail app shows
here too, and nothing you sent disappears when you restart.

features.title: Files in conversations
features.what:
Attach a file to a message: the chip shows its name and size before you send,
you can remove it, and the other side sees a picture inline or a file to open. A file
too large for a message is refused with a message rather than silently dropped.

features.title: Find a conversation
features.what:
Type in the box above the list and it narrows to conversations whose name or
last message matches, including the text of encrypted messages, which your
device reads for itself. The sort button cycles latest, oldest and unread first.

features.title: Format your messages
features.what:
Bold, italic, code, links, headings and lists from a toolbar while you type, offered
as far as the conversation's network can carry them. The conversation list shows plain
text, and the message itself renders formatted.

features.title: Group conversations
features.what:
Add a person to a conversation and it becomes a group; groups can be renamed.
Adding someone to an existing group brings them in without starting over, and
taking someone out removes them from what the group says next.

features.title: Images and video in posts
features.what:
Attach a picture or a video and it shows in the post: pictures inline with a
tap-to-enlarge view, videos as a thumbnail that plays in place when you tap it
(never on its own). Pictures carry their provenance badge when the file has one.
The hidden tags a camera writes into a photo — where it was taken, when, on what
— are removed on your own device, before the picture is ever sent. A picture
linked from somewhere else on the internet stays blocked until you choose to
load it, so the site hosting it does not learn you read the post.

features.goal: docs/goal/architecture/security.md § App display of unverified content
features.guide: docs/guides/who-can-see-what.md § Public posts and your profile
features.title: Know where a post came from
features.what:
Small badges on a post tell you what you are looking at: which network it came
through, whether your app could verify who signed it, whether it was written through
a connected third-party app, and any content label attached to it.

features.title: Like, reply, repost and quote
features.what:
Every post has the four buttons: like, reply, repost and quote, each with its
count. Like and repost toggle back off; a reply or a quote is a post of your own,
and the counts on the original move as you act.

features.goal: docs/goal/architecture/render-model.md § D4 — Link previews — a new async-resolved embed node
features.title: Link previews
features.what:
A bare link in a post or a message grows a preview card with the page's title
and description. Your nest fetches the page, not your device, so the site never sees
you, and the preview image stays off until you ask for it.

features.guide: docs/guides/identity-and-devices.md § If a device is lost or stolen
features.title: Loud warnings when something is very wrong
features.what:
Some things are too important for a page you might never open: someone has
started replacing your recovery kit, your domain is about to lapse, your hosted
AT Protocol identity was moved. The app checks for these every time it starts
and shows a banner on every page until the condition clears; it never treats
"could not check" as "all clear".

features.title: Notifications
features.what:
Notifications list what happened, each with an icon for its kind and an unread
badge in the navigation. New ones arrive while you watch, and one tap marks them all
read.

features.title: Post to a room
features.what:
When you write a post, the audience picker lists the group conversations you are
in. Pick one and your post is still yours — on your profile, in the feeds of
people who follow you — but its full text and photos open only for that room's
members and, for a community room, its home nest; everyone else sees the teaser
you wrote and a locked card. A member just opens the post to read it, and sees
which room it was for.

features.title: Private conversations
features.what:
Message anyone by handle, on your nest or another. Conversations between people
on Fauna are end-to-end encrypted by default: your nest relays encrypted
messages it cannot read, unless a group chooses to be a community room, which
its home nest can read. Every bubble shows who wrote it and when, your history
is there after a restart and on your other devices, and a message that could not
be sent tells you so.

features.title: React to messages and delete your own
features.what:
Every encrypted message has a menu with quick reactions, and your own messages
can be deleted, leaving **This message was deleted** in its place for everyone
in the conversation. Mail messages, which cannot carry reactions, offer neither.

features.title: Read your feed
features.what:
Your feed shows posts newest first, formatted the way they were written, and
opening a post shows it in full. If your connection drops and comes back, the feed
catches up on its own; nothing waits for you to pull.

features.title: Ready for new conversations
features.what:
The people you let reach you can start an encrypted conversation with you at
any time, even while your devices are off: your app keeps a supply of one-use
starter keys waiting on your nest, and tops it up each time you sign in. The Encryption page in Settings shows how many are left, warns
you when the supply runs low, and tops it up when you ask.

features.title: Replies, recipients and threads
features.what:
Replying quotes the message you answer. On a mail conversation you choose who
the reply goes to, reply-all included; on an encrypted conversation the group is the
audience. Mail with a subject threads by subject, and a change of subject shows as a
divider inside the thread.

web.4: docs/goal/behavior/content-index.md § Where queries run — per app
web.8: docs/goal/behavior/content-index.md § Where queries run — per app

features.title: Search
features.what:
One search box finds posts, people and files. Results open where they live: a
post in its detail, a person on their card, a file in Media. Long result lists load
more on demand. People and files are found through the private index your own
devices keep, so in the web app, which keeps none, search finds posts.

features.title: Search within a feed
features.what:
Type in the search box above a feed and it narrows to matching posts by text or
tag; clear it and the full feed is back.

absences.web: docs/goal/behavior/content-index.md § Where queries run — per app

features.title: Search your own mail and files, privately, on this device
features.what:
Your mail is indexed on your own devices from its decrypted contents, and your
files by their names, so the same search box finds a phrase inside a message
stored encrypted on your nest. The index travels between your devices encrypted,
and your nest cannot read it, apart from the part covering your mail, which it
can open with the password of a mail, calendar, contacts or file app you
connect, and only for that app's signed-in session.

features.title: See what is trending
features.what:
A built-in Trending feed shows public posts that are gathering attention, on
your nest and on the nests it federates with. Staying on Trending survives the feed
refreshing.

features.title: See your formatting as you type
features.what:
The reply box shows your formatting while you write it: bold looks bold, code is
monospace, headings are larger and quotes are indented. The marks that make it so stay
out of sight until your cursor moves into the phrase they wrap, and a toolbar toggle
brings them all back for that box. What you typed is exactly what gets sent.

features.guide: docs/guides/app-tour.md § When the app cannot reach your nest
features.title: The app tells you what needs a connection
features.what:
When your nest is out of reach the app keeps working for everything it can do
locally, greys out the controls that need the nest and says why beside each one,
and shows the connection state at the top of the app. The moment the nest is
back, everything comes alive again.

features.title: Unfinished posts, messages and events survive a restart
features.what:
Half-written text is never lost: a post, a message or a calendar event you were
in the middle of is there again after you quit and reopen the app, and on your other
devices too. Cancelling a new conversation discards its draft on purpose. A file
you attached to an unfinished post comes back by name, and posting it asks you to
attach the file again rather than posting without it.

features.title: Unread count on your home screen
features.what:
Fauna shows how many unread messages are waiting for you without your opening
the app: in a widget on your phone's home screen or your Mac's desktop, and as a
count on the app's own icon on Windows and Linux. It keeps itself up to date in
the background.

features.title: Write a post
features.what:
Write a post from the bar at the top of your feed or open the full editor for
longer pieces. Tags become chips, files attach from the composer, and what you
publish shows up in your feed at once.

features.title: Your profile and other people's
features.what:
Edit your display name, avatar and banner: everyone on your nest sees them,
people on other nests do too once you turn on **People on other nests can see
your profile**, and, whatever that switch says, so do people on the Fediverse
once you enable it and on Bluesky when your nest hosts your Bluesky identity.
Open another person's profile from your contacts to message them, subscribe to
what they offer, or block them.

features.guide: docs/guides/identity-and-devices.md § Where the key lives — and where you should put a copy
features.title: A copy of your identity in your cloud keychain
features.what:
On iPhone and Mac you can choose to keep a copy of your identity in your iCloud
Keychain as well as on the device. It is off until you turn it on, so by default
your identity stays out of iCloud. With it on, a new iPhone or Mac restored from
your Apple account, with iCloud Keychain on, finds your identity when the app
first starts there. Turning it off removes the copy from iCloud Keychain and
nothing more: every device that already has your identity keeps it. Adding a
device and your recovery kit remain the main ways to have your identity in more
than one place; the cloud copy is an extra you can opt into.

features.guide: docs/guides/identity-and-devices.md § Several identities on one device
features.title: A second identity in its own window
features.what:
On the desktop, open a second identity in a window of its own and use both at
once. Launching the app while it is already open offers to pick an identity or
takes you straight back to what is running; two windows never fight over one
identity.

features.guide: docs/guides/cloud-photos.md § Automatic photo backup from your phone
features.title: Back up your photos
features.what:
On a phone, your photo library is a backup folder: new photos flow to your nest
by themselves and are there to browse from any device, without the phone ever giving
up its own copies.

features.guide: docs/guides/cloud-backup.md § Backup destinations: surviving the loss of the nest itself
features.title: Backup destinations and restore
features.what:
Your nest can copy its encrypted backups somewhere else: another nest, yours or
a friend's, or a device of yours. Another nest cannot read what it holds, apart
from a folder you have made public; a copy on a device of yours can be read by
anyone who can unlock that device. The Backups page shows when each destination
last received a copy, audits it and warns when one goes dark or its store rots,
restores your mail from a snapshot your nest keeps, with a history of every
restore, and, if you lose your nest, brings your mail, calendar, contacts and
posts, and any folder you attached, back from a destination's copy — from
another nest's copy once the lost nest is rebuilt with its own identity; a
folder's own settings attach a destination to it.

features.guide: docs/guides/cloud-backup.md § Snapshots: the time machine on your nest
features.title: Backups: snapshots
features.what:
Every folder keeps snapshots on your nest. Browse a snapshot's files, download
a single file exactly as it was, check a snapshot's integrity, prune old ones with a
preview first, recover one you pruned, and see when a folder was last backed up.
Deleting a snapshot for good needs a typed confirmation.

features.title: Choose which device does the heavy lifting
features.what:
Some jobs, like building your search index, should run on exactly one of your
devices. The Task delegation page shows each job, which device is doing it right now,
and lets you pin one to a particular device or leave it automatic; automatic works with no
set-up at all.

features.title: Connected apps
features.what:
One page lists everything that acts for you from outside Fauna: websites you signed
in to, apps on your other devices, apps using one of your app passwords, the Nostr
apps your nest signs for. Each row says what the app may reach in plain words, and
you disconnect it there. You connect an app on another device by typing the code it
shows you, an app on this device hands you a link that opens its request here, and a
request from an app you have never approved waits quietly on this page instead of
interrupting you.

features.title: Direct connections between your devices
features.what:
The Linux app has a page for looking into direct device-to-device connections:
start and stop a test tunnel that carries none of your files, copy this device's
address and its addresses on the local network, and see and remove the devices
it has talked to. Your files never wait on that page: where your devices pass
files to each other directly, they do it in the background, and each device's
**Peer transfers** switch is on its card on the **Devices** page. The transfers
themselves are described in [Files move straight between your own
devices](device-to-device-file-transfer.md), and handing a folder to someone
else in person is [Share a folder in person, with no nest in
between](offline-sharing.md).

features.guide: docs/guides/your-own-cloud.md § The trust model, in plain words
features.title: Export everything
features.what:
One button in Settings gives you an archive of everything your nest holds for
you.

features.title: fauna-for-ai-assistants
features.what: This text is being written and will appear here once it has been reviewed.

features.title: Files move straight between your own devices
features.what:
When two of your devices are on the same network, a file syncing between them
travels directly from one to the other instead of through your nest, so it
arrives faster and your nest never sees its contents. There is nothing to set
up and nothing to switch on, and if the direct path is ever unavailable the
file still arrives the ordinary way, through your nest.

This is about your own devices passing your own files to each other; handing a
folder to someone else in person is [Share a folder in person, with no nest in
between](offline-sharing.md).

features.title: Files on demand
features.what:
Where the operating system has cloud files, a synced folder can show every file
as a placeholder that downloads when you open it, so a big folder takes no space
until you need it. It is still two-way: a file you change uploads all the same.

features.title: Folders
features.what:
A folder holds files your nest looks after; it has no fixed type: you say what
each of your devices does with it and who can see it. Make one in a short
wizard, choose which of your devices take part and how, decide how many copies
the nest keeps and whether it keeps the files' contents at all or only passes
them between your devices, and see what each device changed. Conflicts resolve
on their own and land on a review list, with a policy you choose per folder.

features.title: Follow someone's public folder
features.what:
Follow a folder someone made public by their handle and the folder's name, and
browse it in Media as a read-only folder, even when it lives on another nest. If
they take it private again, your copy stops updating.

features.title: Keep a folder on your computer in sync
features.what:
Bind a folder on your computer — your own, or one a friend shared with you as a
writer — and a small helper keeps it in sync in the background: a file you drop in
is on your nest and on your other computers moments later, edits and deletes travel
both ways, and a folder that vanishes wholesale is held for your say-so rather than
deleted everywhere. The app shows the helper's health, and changing which folders
sync takes effect at once.

features.title: Make a folder public, or a website
features.what:
A folder is private until you say otherwise. Make it public, after an explicit
confirmation, and anyone can read it; turn on the website switch and your nest
serves its files at your address. Turning the folder back from public stops the
serving at once, and your devices encrypt what it holds again, what it held
while public included; but treat anything you published as public for good. The
devices of people you shared it with never make anything public: what they add
stays encrypted while the folder is public and afterwards.

features.title: Privacy: who can reach you, and your spam threshold
features.what:
Choose who may start a conversation with you: anyone, contacts only, or nobody.
Contacts only isn't applied yet to someone on another nest who starts a
conversation with you, unless they do it by inviting you to a room. Set how
aggressive your spam filter is and whether your training helps others. Both
persist across relaunch and show the real value, never a default — and while
your nest is still being asked, the page says so rather than marking a guess.

features.guide: docs/guides/who-can-see-what.md § Public posts and your profile
features.title: Publish to the web
features.what:
Publish a post to the open web from its menu and copy a link that loads for
anyone; unpublish it from Settings. Opt into your own subdomain and your
published posts serve there. A paywalled post gets a link that unlocks the full
text for the holder once you have let your nest serve that tier's paywalled
posts (**Settings → Nests**); a nest with no serving domain says so instead of
handing you a dead link.

features.title: Run a job on this device
features.what:
On the Task delegation page, a job this computer can run offers *This device*
beside the automatic choice. Choose it and the job stays here: the pin is
remembered across restarts and on every device you own, and clearing it hands
the job back to automatic. Phones, tablets and the web app run no heavy jobs,
so they never offer it; on them the page still shows which device is doing
each job.

features.guide: docs/guides/identity-and-devices.md § Several identities on one device
features.title: Several identities in one app
features.what:
Add a second identity and switch between them from Settings; each keeps its own
conversations, files and settings, and removing one never touches the others. An
identity you mark as protected asks you to confirm before it activates, and the
nest's admin identity is protected by default. Abandoning an add halfway leaves the
identity you had.

features.guide: docs/guides/cloud-sharing-family.md § Sharing a folder with someone
features.title: Share a folder in person, with no nest in between
features.what:
Two people sitting together can share a folder device to device: each copies the
other's code from the screen in front of them, one gets ready to receive, the
other begins, and the folder is listed on both sides. Copying the folder's files
across this way is still being built; in a folder you share through your nest, a
file added while the nest is unreachable can already reach the other person
straight from your device. Nobody can start a share with you that you did not
ask for. This is about giving a folder to another person face to face; your own
devices moving your own files between themselves is [Files move straight between
your own devices](device-to-device-file-transfer.md).

features.guide: docs/guides/cloud-sharing-family.md § Sharing a folder with someone
features.title: Share a folder with people
features.what:
Share a folder with someone, on your nest or another, as a reader or a writer;
they accept or decline, and a writer can add files. What they receive is
encrypted with a key only members hold, and a member's own app opens it. Making
the folder public changes that, as [Make a folder public, or a
website](public-folders-and-websites.md) explains; if you serve it over WebDAV
or put it behind a paywall, the box that serves it can read it too. A folder can
also be served to standard file apps over WebDAV; its files stay stored
encrypted on your nest, which opens them with the password of a mail, calendar,
contacts or file app you connect, for that app's signed-in session.

features.title: Share a link to a file
features.what:
Make a link to a file and send it to anyone: they open it in an ordinary
browser, with no account. A file in a folder you have made public is served as
it is; a file in a folder only you can open, and not served over WebDAV, stays
encrypted on your nest, and the link itself carries the key that opens it. Each
link expires after the time you choose, and you can see every link you have made
and revoke any of them, after which it stops working for everyone.

features.title: Start at login and close to tray
features.what:
On the desktop the app can start when you sign in, and closing its window is
never a silent stop: the app keeps running in the tray where there is one, sync
carries on where its background sync helper keeps running after the window
closes, and where nothing can stay behind, closing quits and the setting says
so. Close to tray is on by default wherever there is a tray, and start at login
is on by default on every desktop (you can turn either off, and the app keeps
your choice).

features.title: Status, quotas and limits
features.what:
The Status page shows how much of your quota you use and every limit that
applies to you, which feature it binds, how much headroom is left, and who set it,
in readable units. No limit is ever silent.

features.guide: docs/guides/identity-and-devices.md § If a device is lost or stolen
features.title: Take your account back
features.what:
If your identity key is stolen, the recovery kit moves your account to a fresh
identity the thief cannot follow: the old key stops working, at your nest at
once and at each other nest your account is linked to once one of your devices
next syncs with it; your groups move with you (and if some do not, you can
finish moving them yourself); and any device still on the old key is told what
happened and asked to import the new one. Your data, backups, conversations,
drafts and mail come back under the new key, the old mail passwords stop
working, and anything the thief could have changed is raised for your review.

features.title: The app's own log
features.what:
Settings has a Logs page with what the app has been doing, newest first,
filterable by severity, with copy and clear. Any error the app showed you is in
there too, so you can hand it to whoever helps you. On a computer or a phone the
same log is also kept in a file of its own on the device, so what happened
before a crash or a restart is not lost with the page.

features.title: Where you are signed in
features.what:
The Sessions page shows every place your account is signed in right now, with
this app's own sign-in first, and lets you end any other one, or all of them at
once, while saying plainly that ending a sign-in does not sign a device out and
where the real remedies are. It also offers the 24-hour emergency lock.

features.title: Your account: handle, sign out, delete
features.what:
Change your handle, see and copy your identity, sign out, or delete the
account. Changes that matter take effect after a delay and stay cancellable in the
meantime, in a section that shows everything pending. Signing out wipes every
credential from the device.

features.title: Your devices
features.what:
The Devices page lists every device signed in as you, exactly as your nest
knows them, marks the one you are holding, shows which folders each takes part in,
and lets you remove one. Your own identity is one tap away to hand to a new device.

features.goal: docs/goal/architecture/account-sync-plane.md § The peer leg — device↔device sync over iroh (requirement 7)
features.title: devices-in-step-without-the-nest
features.what: This text is being written and will appear here once it has been reviewed.

features.guide: docs/guides/identity-and-devices.md § Where the key lives — and where you should put a copy
features.title: Your identity encrypted with a passphrase
features.what: Where the app has no protected store of the device's own to keep your identity in — the terminal app on a server or over SSH, or on a computer whose system keyring is locked or not set up, and the web app in any browser — Fauna keeps your identity encrypted with a passphrase you choose. You choose it before you set anything up, typing it twice, and the app asks for it again before it opens anything; in a browser, a new tab asks nothing while another Fauna tab is already open. What you type never shows, a wrong passphrase is refused, and you can change the passphrase from Settings without being signed out; the app reminds you to back up your identity first, because nobody can reset a forgotten passphrase — your identity then comes back from your recovery kit, an exported copy of your key, or another device where you're signed in. In the web app you can also start over from the unlock screen: that erases this browser's copy of your keys and nothing else. In a browser and on a device that support it, with the web app opened at your nest's name over HTTPS rather than at a bare IP address, you can also add a passkey that unlocks your encrypted identity with your device's screen lock or a security key; the passphrase keeps working. However the app stops, whatever it finds it cannot read, and however many copies of it are open, your encrypted identity is never cut short, emptied or lost. On a computer or phone that keeps your identity in its own protected store instead, there is no passphrase to choose.

features.guide: docs/guides/identity-and-devices.md § Where the key lives — and where you should put a copy
features.title: Your identity is kept safe on this device
features.what:
Your identity is a secret key, and each device you use keeps its own copy where that device protects secrets — the keychain on iPhone and Mac, the equivalent stores on Windows, Linux and Android. Where there is no such store — in the web app, and in the terminal app on a server or over SSH, or on a computer whose system keyring is locked or not set up — the app asks you to choose a passphrase the first time it opens and keeps the key encrypted with it, asking for the passphrase again at each launch (in a browser, once per session, as long as one Fauna tab stays open). Either way, reopening the app finds your identity where you left it: nothing to set up twice. Where the key is encrypted with a passphrase, you can change that passphrase from Settings, and the old one stops opening it.

The app never sends your key anywhere by itself — not into a backup, not into a sync between your devices. It leaves a device only when you move it yourself: by adding a device, exporting your identity, making a recovery kit, or — on iPhone and Mac — turning on the iCloud Keychain backup. What your device's own backup then does with the place the key is kept depends on the device: some keep the key on the device and out of the backup, others carry it still locked under your sign-in password or your passphrase — and a copy of your browser's data carries it encrypted with your passphrase, too.

features.guide: docs/guides/nest-relay-setup.md § Step 1 — Link the two nests
features.title: Your nests and what each may read
features.what:
Link another nest of yours so your account lives on both, and see on the Nests
page what each nest is trusted to read: every permission you gave it, its
expiry, its history, and a revoke for each. Backup destinations and past backup
generations show there too, and the admin can refuse linking altogether.

features.title: Your recovery kit
features.what:
Make a recovery kit from Settings: a second key, shown once, that can restore
your account after you have lost every device, or replace a kit you already
hold. A kit you copied from Settings says where your account lives; with one
made at sign-up, or a code you typed, the restore asks for your handle; your
secret key's link or QR, pasted where the kit belongs, is refused.

features.guide: docs/guides/own-your-mail.md § Moving in from your old provider
features.title: Bring your mail from another provider
features.what:
Move your existing mail — from Gmail, iCloud or any other IMAP server, and from
Outlook once your nest's admin has entered a Microsoft app registration — into
your own mailbox without leaving the app. A short wizard asks where your mail
is, lets you choose which mailboxes to bring and from what date, shows you how
much is coming before you start, and then shows its progress as the mail
arrives. Your old provider's password stays in your app: your nest never sees
it. Mailboxes, dates and read, flagged and answered marks come across as they
were — a Gmail message filed under several labels lands once — and mail you
already have is not copied twice.

features.guide: docs/guides/own-your-mail.md § Addresses: aliases, plus-addresses, and role addresses
features.title: Mail aliases
features.what:
Give out as many addresses as you like: exact aliases, a wildcard prefix,
disposable addresses made in one tap, and a list you paste in at once. Switch
one off and back on, set how much mail an alias may receive, and keep your
primary address, which cannot be removed.

features.title: Mail filter rules
features.what:
Rules that file, drop, forward or auto-reply to mail as it arrives, made and
edited in Settings. They run on the nest, so they apply whichever mail app you read
with, and an auto-reply answers each sender once and never answers a machine.

features.title: Mailing lists
features.what:
Run a newsletter from your own address: make a list, add members one at a time
or by pasting a block, and send. Every message carries a one-click unsubscribe that
works, an unsubscribed member stays on the list as unsubscribed, and sends are
capped so one list cannot burn your domain's reputation.

features.title: Spam, your way
features.what:
A spam filter of your own, trained by you: mark a message as spam and it learns,
undo a lesson, reset it, and see its history. Scoring runs on your device or in the
mail server before a message is ever shown, so spam lands in Junk on every mail app.
You can contribute your training to the nest's shared starting point, and share what
you report with other nests, in anonymous aggregate only.

features.guide: docs/guides/own-your-mail.md § Taking your mail with you
features.title: Take your mailbox with you
features.what:
Walk a five-step wizard and your whole mailbox comes back to you as one archive
file — in mbox, Maildir++ or a folder of `.eml` files, whichever your next mail
app reads. Pick which mailboxes, narrow it to a date range, and strip the
transit headers if you would rather not carry them. Nobody who runs the server
can read the archive on its way to you: it is encrypted to a key only your
devices hold, and it stays that way until it lands on your own disk.

features.title: Turn on mail for your account
features.what:
On a nest set up without mail, the page says so and the switch stays off;
otherwise, one switch gives you a mailbox at your own address. The page then
shows the settings a regular mail app needs, lists the app passwords you have
made, shows each one again on request, lets you add and revoke them, rotate the
keys behind them, and turn mail off again. A new member gets mail from their
first sign-in when the admin allows it, and turning mail on in the app also
starts the mail server on the nest.

features.guide: docs/guides/own-your-mail.md § Connecting a regular mail app
features.title: Use a regular mail app
features.what:
Thunderbird, Apple Mail or any IMAP client reads and sends your mail with the
address and app password the Fauna app shows you: one password for reading,
sending and your calendar alike, a second password if you want one, and mail
that reaches your inbox the moment it arrives. Mail your nest passes to and from
email is readable to it on the way, as on every mail server, and is stored
encrypted as it lands; after that, your nest opens it with the password of a
mail, calendar, contacts or file app you connect, and only for that app's
signed-in session; beyond those, your nest reads it for itself only if you give
it permission to read your mail, or you subscribe to a community labeler that
reads your mail, which gets its own trust for that one labeler and your mail
alone. Your nest also sees what any server that delivers your messages must: who
you're connected to — your contacts, whom you follow, the groups you're in — and
when and how much you send.

features.guide: docs/guides/calendar-and-contacts.md § Contacts: two different address books, on purpose
features.title: Your address book in standard contacts apps
features.what:
Any CardDAV contacts app connects with the same address and app password, finds
your address book from the server name alone, and reads and writes cards stored
encrypted on your nest, which opens them with the password of a mail, calendar,
contacts or file app you connect, and only for that app's signed-in session;
beyond that, no permission you give your nest lets it read your address book.
Your nest also sees what any server that delivers your messages must: who you're
connected to — your contacts, whom you follow, the groups you're in — and when
and how much you send.

features.goal: docs/goal/behavior/mail-multidomain.md § The model: one handle, addressable on every active domain
features.title: your-address-on-every-domain
features.what: This text is being written and will appear here once it has been reviewed.

features.guide: docs/guides/calendar-and-contacts.md § Connecting Apple Calendar, Thunderbird, DAVx⁵…
features.title: Your calendar in Apple Calendar, Thunderbird and friends
features.what:
Any CalDAV calendar app connects with your address and app password, finds your
calendars by itself, adds new ones, and sees an event the moment you make it in
the Fauna app. Invitations you send from any of them reach the attendees,
including people on other nests and people with no mailbox, and their replies
come back. Events are stored encrypted on your nest, which opens them with the
password of a mail, calendar, contacts or file app you connect, and only for
that app's signed-in session. Invitations and replies that travel by email are
readable to your nest as they pass to and from email, like any mail; beyond
those, your nest reads your calendar itself only if you give it permission to
read your calendar. Your nest also sees what any server that delivers your
messages must: who you're connected to — your contacts, whom you follow, the
groups you're in — and when and how much you send.

features.guide: docs/guides/cloud-sync.md § Mount it like a network drive (WebDAV)
features.title: Your folders as a network drive
features.what:
Mount a served folder in your file manager over WebDAV with your app password:
list, read and write files. They stay stored encrypted on your nest, which opens
them with the password of a mail, calendar, contacts or file app you connect,
for that app's signed-in session. A folder you have not served stays
unreachable, and the mail-app settings page shows the address to mount.

features.guide: docs/guides/bridges-bluesky-nostr.md § Bluesky, the destination: your nest as your Bluesky home
features.title: AT Protocol
features.what:
Choose how deep Bluesky goes: off, your existing account linked, or your nest as
your Bluesky home — visible to the network, or with full access, so other
Bluesky apps sign in through it. Each step up shows what it will do before you
confirm. App passwords and third-party posting are yours to grant and revoke;
the app watches the public directory for anyone trying to take your identity and
can contest it.

features.title: Bring your posts from Facebook
features.what:
Download the export archive Facebook gives you and bring it into Fauna from the
app; importing Instagram archives is planned. Your posts and albums come back at the dates they happened — unless you choose Only me, a public one can be seen on Fauna, a Friends-only one by the people who follow you, and any other only by you — each marked with the service it came from, and your events land in your
own calendar. The untouched archive is stored encrypted in a folder on your
nest, so nothing in it is lost. Other people's comments, and your message
threads, stay in the archive for you alone and are never published; showing them
in the app is planned, and so is linking with a friend who also imported, so
that your comments and reactions on each other's posts come back, each signed by
the person who wrote it.

features.title: Link other networks
features.what:
The Bridges page links your account to other networks and unlinks it again. A
bridge that cannot be linked right now says why instead of offering a dead button.
Once a bridge is on, you can subscribe a feed of yours to a source on that network,
and only the bridges your nest can actually serve are offered.

features.guide: docs/guides/bridges-bluesky-nostr.md § Nostr: a personal Nostr home
features.title: Nostr
features.what:
Link a Nostr key, or let the app make one, and choose what cross-publishes.
Manage your relays and the people you follow, connect other Nostr apps through your
nest as their signer, and name the signers whose zap receipts you believe.

features.title: The fediverse
features.what:
Turn federation on and you have a fediverse address. People on Mastodon and
its relatives follow you and get your posts, their favourites and boosts show on your
posts, deleting a post takes it back from them, and you follow accounts there and
read their posts in your feed. Your reply to a fediverse post, or your quote of
one, reaches its author.

features.guide: docs/guides/who-can-see-what.md § Paid posts — what is public and what is not
features.title: Gated posts, sold posts and tips
features.what:
Gate a post to a tier as you write it, or sell a single post for a price shown
on its teaser; a buyer unlocks it, and an existing subscriber reads it free. A folder
on the web can be paywalled the same way. Tips on a post show their total and who
gave them.

features.guide: docs/guides/install.md § Checking you have the official app
features.title: store-install
features.what: This text is being written and will appear here once it has been reviewed.

features.guide: docs/guides/who-can-see-what.md § Paid posts — what is public and what is not
features.title: Subscribe to creators; offer tiers of your own
features.what:
Offer tiers from your profile and see who subscribes; subscribe to someone
else's from theirs, and their posts for that tier unlock for you. A follow unlocks by
itself; a paid tier is granted the moment the payment arrives, through a payment
provider you connect or a code you hand out by hand. Your active subscriptions are
listed in Settings, where you also unsubscribe.

features.title: Community labelers
features.what:
Browse labelers other people published, inspect what one does before you
subscribe, and see your subscriptions on the Personalization page. You can sort
the posts you see according to labelers you subscribe to. A labeler that needs a
newer app says so, on its row or when you inspect it, and cannot be subscribed
to.

features.title: Correct the classifier
features.what:
Your own moderation queue shows what your device flagged, including spam
detected in an encrypted message after it was decrypted, and lets you correct the
classifier. Where an admin — of your nest, or of another nest that shows your post or is the home nest of a community room you are in — has acted on your content under a legal obligation, the queue also shows that decision, says which nest made it when it was another nest, and lets you appeal it with a reason, which goes on that nest's record for an admin to review. Below the
queue, the page lists the reports you made about other people's content and lets
you withdraw one while it is still open.

features.guide: docs/guides/cloud-sharing-family.md § A family on one nest
features.title: kids-app
features.what: This text is being written and will appear here once it has been reviewed.

features.title: Learn from my activity
features.what:
Let a topic learn from what you actually linger on: a switch per topic, with a
button to clear what it collected. Optionally share your signals on public posts in
anonymous aggregate, and see the anonymous counts your nest shares with other nests.

features.title: Muted words
features.what: Words you mute collapse any post, message or notification that contains them behind a reveal — in every feed and conversation and in your notifications, on all your devices; a security notice always shows in full. A word you would rather see less of than not at all can instead only sink matching posts in your ranked feeds.

features.title: Report a post, a message or an account
features.what:
Tell your nest's administrators about a post, a message someone sent you, or an
account you think they should see. You pick a reason, can add a note, and can block
the person in the same step. A private message stays private unless you tick the box
that attaches its text. When the person lives on another nest, your report is passed
on to that nest's administrators too, without your name. A report removes nothing by itself, and the person you report is never told who reported them; what changes is your own view, where what you reported is replaced by a note that you reported it. You are told what became of your report, and the Moderation page (in the web app, a section of Settings → Privacy) lists your reports and lets you withdraw one while it is still open.

features.guide: docs/guides/cloud-sharing-family.md § A family on one nest
features.title: Supervised accounts for children
features.what:
A guardian supervises a child's account: sees it on the Family page, decides
whether unknown people may message the child, approves the contacts the child asks
for, blocks content categories on the child's feed and conversations, hears how
often that fired, sets screen-time windows and a daily budget, and marks the
child's devices. Guardianship can be handed to another adult who must agree first.
Mail to a supervised child is gated at the nest.

features.title: Train your own topics
features.what:
Make a topic, tell it "more like this" on a post, and the feeds you weight it
into re-rank; the examples and the model survive a restart. A topic you trained
can be published as a labeler for others, as a list of posts or as a
word-pattern model that also matches posts nobody here has seen yet. People who
subscribe to it can sort the posts they see according to it.

features.title: region-rules
features.what: This text is being written and will appear here once it has been reviewed.

features.title: Aliases that forward outside
features.what:
Give an address on your domain to someone with no mailbox here: mail to it
forwards to their address elsewhere. A target on a domain you host is refused,
because that would be an alias, not a forward.

features.title: Bridges: approve and rotate keys
features.what:
The nest's own mail helpers enrol themselves and are approved by themselves once
mail is on; anything else, the Bluesky helper included, waits here for you. Each approved helper
shows what it does, and its key can be rotated in one click with a warning about
what that costs.

features.title: Calendar, Contacts and Files switches
features.what:
Three switches turn calendar, contacts and file serving on or off for the whole
nest, independent of mail, plus the port calendar, contacts and file apps use
when they reach the nest directly at its own address — a nest at home or on a
desktop computer; on a server in the cloud with a domain, all three are served
at the domain's mail server name on the standard port, 443. Where the port
applies, changing it moves the live listener; a calendar app keeps working on
the new one.

features.title: Domains, DNS records and certificates
features.what:
One page lists every domain the nest hosts and every DNS record each needs,
with the exact value and whether it is live. Add a domain and it gets its records,
its keys and, once DNS is right, a real certificate; remove one and restore it within
a month. Hand the app a DNS provider credential, which never leaves your device, and
it publishes the records for you and renews certificates by DNS. Each domain has a
catch-all member, overrides for the standard role addresses, and a certificate
badge; the primary domain can be renamed.

features.title: Factory reset and set up again
features.what:
Factory reset wipes the nest and hands you a fresh claim code, pre-filled in
the app, so you can set it up again with the same identity; mail and calendars
come back working. Whatever the app was doing when it crashed, the nest is left in
a state the app can recover from, with no command line involved.

features.title: Held Custody: encrypted copies kept for people elsewhere
features.what:
A page listing the encrypted copies this nest keeps for people from other nests,
which it cannot read apart from anything they have published to everyone, honest
when there are none.

features.title: Logs
features.what:
The nest's recent activity, newest first, filterable by severity, with copy. The
nest's helpers report their events into the same log. Below it, the record of
admin actions — who did what, newest first — and whether the entries shown check
out.

features.title: Mail health at a glance
features.what:
At the top of the Mail page, right under the mail on/off switch, one line says
whether mail is working — delivering, warming up, delayed, blocklisted, records
needing attention, the mail service not connected, or simply off — followed by
when mail was last delivered and last received. Seven short rows underneath show
each check behind that line. **Check again** re-runs the blocklist and
DNS-record checks on the spot; **Restart warm-up** (after the server's outgoing
address changed) asks you to press again before it starts the sending ramp over.
While the server's address is on a blocklist, a link to request removal
appears. The same one-line state shows as a **Mail** card on the dashboard, so a
problem is visible the moment you open the admin area.

features.title: Mail policy
features.what:
One flat form sets the mail server's policy: whether new members get mail by
themselves, the spam thresholds and how much the shared filter trusts training, the
penalty for mail to an unlisted address, connection limits, the idle timeout, alias
caps, and a button that publishes the nest's shared spam baseline once enough people
contribute. A change applies to the running server without a restart.

features.title: Members: requests, registration, invites and actions
features.what:
One page for who is on, who wants on and how to let someone on: approve join
requests at a tier, create invite codes, admit someone directly by their account
key, change a member's tier, suspend them at once, which you can undo, or evict
them with a countdown you can call off until the deletion starts, and hand out
or take back the admin role, never leaving the nest with no admin. You set
whether registration is open, invite-only or closed, right here.

features.title: Nest: network mode, pairing, ports, updates, region, identity, sign-in keys and takedowns
features.what:
The Nest page holds what applies to the whole nest: whether it is public or
behind a home router, whether other nests may link to it, the port it serves on,
pending operating-system updates with a restart button, the region it declares,
a deliberate rotation of the nest's own identity that every app follows silently,
the keys outside apps' sign-ins are signed with — replaced as a precaution or at once
after a leak, each control saying what it costs first — and a legal takedown of a
post that you can overturn.

features.guide: docs/guides/admin-tour.md § Getting in — and back out
features.title: The admin area
features.what:
If you are the nest's admin, the app shows an Admin entry that others never
see. It opens a separate area with its own navigation, a dashboard of member and
version counts, and one way back out. A failed admin action tells you on the page it
happened on.

features.title: Tiers and paid membership
features.what:
Tiers set what a member may store and do. Edit each tier's caps in place, and
point paid membership at one of your own subscription tiers so access to the nest
can be sold.

features.title: Web: whose site is the front page
features.what:
Pick one member whose published site serves at the nest's bare address, and
clear the choice again.

features.title: A home nest behind a public relay
features.what:
Keep your data at home and still receive mail at a domain: a small public nest
takes your mail in, stores it encrypted until the home nest collects it, and, as
long as you have not given it permission to read your mail, keeps no readable
copy of the mail you receive. The two link from the app in one step.

features.guide: docs/guides/who-can-see-what.md § Your handle, your domains, and security certificates
features.title: Certificates, by themselves
features.what:
There is nothing to choose to get this: your nest serves an encrypted connection from its first
second, on a certificate it made itself, and a nest the internet can reach swaps in
a publicly trusted one once its domain resolves to it, with no restart, for the
nest, for mail and for calendars alike. A nest the certificate authority cannot
reach — a home nest, or one whose web port is blocked — gets its trusted
certificate through the admin's app instead. The mail records that tell other servers which certificate
to expect always follow the one actually served.

features.guide: docs/guides/own-your-mail.md § Addresses: aliases, plus-addresses, and role addresses
features.title: DMARC reports are read for you, not mailed to you
features.what:
There is nothing to choose to get this. Every domain your nest serves asks the big mail providers for a daily report
on who sent mail in its name. Those reports come back to your nest, which reads
them itself and keeps them for 90 days. They never land in anyone's inbox. A
broken report, or one about a domain your nest does not serve, is dropped
quietly, and the provider that sent it is never told to retry.

Three things are an admin's to choose, on the mail admin page: how long the reports are kept; whether to also ask providers for *forensic* reports — one per failed message, naming the people it was sent to; and whether your nest sends reports of its own. Forensic reports are off unless an admin turns them on, and the switch says what they carry. Your nest's own reports go once a day to each domain that asks for them in its DMARC record, about the mail it received claiming to be from that domain; they are on unless an admin switches off **Send daily DMARC reports to other domains**.

An admin reads the daily reports on the Mail reports page: the totals for a period and domain, the busiest sources and senders, and each report in full.

features.goal: docs/goal/architecture/security.md § Co-resident process trust boundary (UID isolation)
features.guide: docs/guides/your-own-cloud.md § The trust model, in plain words
features.title: Each part of the nest is walled off
features.what:
There is nothing to choose: inside Fauna's container image for the nest every part that talks to the network runs under a system account of its own, the parts that handle mail run in a sandbox, no helper can read another's keys or the nest's encrypted store of your data, a mail helper cannot sign in to the nest under a forged identity, and a mail helper that starts without these walls shows up as a warning in the admin's log in the app, so nobody needs a command line to find out.
A stop is a clean goodbye to every connected app.

features.guide: docs/guides/own-your-mail.md § Why this is normally hard, and what Fauna does about it
features.title: Mail from and to the outside world
features.what:
There is nothing to choose to get this: once mail is on, the nest runs a real mail server. Mail
from anywhere reaches your inbox, mail you send leaves signed so the big providers
accept it, a sender that was told to try again does deliver on the retry, a failed
delivery comes back to you and never to a stranger, and an upgrade never loses a
mailbox. The signing keys are created and rotated by the nest itself. A domain that
asks for a daily report on the mail sent in its name, or on how encrypted delivery
to it went, is sent one. How strict the server is with incoming mail, and whether it
sends those reports, is the admin's to tune in the admin area; the defaults need no
tuning.

features.title: Retire a nest
features.what:
A server your app set up in your cloud account since 8 July 2026 can be taken down from the app too, even when the nest on it no longer answers. You enter your cloud token, see
the servers Fauna created there since 8 July 2026, when it began marking them
(on OVH, every server your credentials reach, each with a note to check its
name), type the name of the one to delete, and the app removes the DNS records
that belong to it before it deletes the server itself — so none of your names
still points at an address your provider may hand to someone else. Where the app
has no access to your DNS, it lists the records for you to remove yourself. If
your domain came from a provider that can hand out its transfer code, the app
fetches that too.

features.guide: docs/guides/own-your-mail.md § Addresses: aliases, plus-addresses, and role addresses
features.title: TLS failure reports are read for you, not mailed to you
features.what:
There is nothing to choose to get this. Every domain your nest serves asks
other mail servers to report when they could not make an encrypted connection
to it. Those daily reports come back to your nest, which reads them itself and
keeps them for 90 days. They never land in anyone's inbox. A broken report, or
one about a domain your nest does not serve, is dropped quietly, and the server
that sent it is never told to retry.

features.title: Upgrades never lose your data
features.what:
From version 0.2.0 on, an older app talks to a newer nest and a newer app to an older nest, in the same major version, and each app's own data opens under the next build and the previous one; during the 0.1 versions an update may need a fresh install of the app or the nest. A nest handed data from a newer, incompatible build stays up but
serves nothing from that data rather than damage it, tells every app it needs an
update, and recovers untouched when the newer build returns. An app that cannot read the list of accounts on
your device never offers to start you over as if you had none.

features.guide: docs/guides/own-your-mail.md § Why this is normally hard, and what Fauna does about it
features.title: Your mail server refuses abuse
features.what:
There is nothing to choose to get this: the mail server cannot be used to relay spam, refuses
mail that forges your own domain, checks the sender's signatures and policy, scans
for malware, and holds a connection storm to a limit, all by default. An admin can
tighten or loosen the checks that have a setting in the admin area's mail policy.

features.title: Your nest relays your devices' direct traffic
features.what:
There is nothing to choose: a nest with a public name of its own runs a relay for your devices'
direct connections, at its own address on the standard port, and tells your apps it
is there. When two of your devices cannot reach each other directly, their traffic
passes through the relay, encrypted from one device to the other, so the relay
cannot read it; where there is no relay, your apps go through the nest as usual.
Only the devices of your nest's own members can use it.

features.goal: docs/goal/behavior/web-content-hosting.md § Serving the SPA is artifact wiring
features.guide: docs/guides/install.md § The no-install option: the web app
features.title: Your nest serves the app
features.what:
There is nothing to choose to get this: Fauna's container image for the nest carries the web app and serves it at the nest's own address, on every start, with the security headers a browser expects.
A nest whose saved settings never recorded where the app is finds it again on the
next restart. An admin can instead send visitors to the Fauna project's own address for the app, with the nest already filled in on the sign-in page, by choosing it under **Web app** in the admin area (a nest without a domain yet keeps serving the app itself); that address serves the app's code and holds nothing of yours, and it is not live yet.
